extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students in analysis (Fourier/Harmonic Analysis) and instructors using a graduate-level textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Statements and usable criteria about Poisson/conjugate Poisson kernels, the Hilbert transform and its approximations, weak-type estimates, Calderón–Zygmund style decompositions, and the basic properties of Lp spaces (Hölder, Minkowski, density, interpolation, completeness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson and conjugate Poisson integrals properties (Theorem 8.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be in L^2(R^1) and let u(x,y) = (P_y * f)(x) and v(x,y) = (Q_y * f)(x) be the Poisson integral and conjugate Poisson integral of f. Then (a) v is harmonic in R^2_+ and the pair u,v satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations; (b) for every ε>0, Q_ε * f is in L^2 and its L^2 Fourier transform satisfies certain bounds; (c) and (d) follow by taking L^2 Fourier transforms and using Plancherel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem provides regularity (harmonicity), Cauchy–Riemann relations, L^2 membership of the conjugate Poisson approximations Q_ε * f for each ε>0, and L^2-limit behavior as ε→0. The proof uses Plancherel, approximation by L^1∩L^2 functions, and dominated convergence / subsequence a.e. convergence to pass to limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete L^2 limit formula for the Hilbert transform (Remark following Theorem 8.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f in L^2(R^1), the Hilbert transform Hf is the L^2-limit as ε↓0 of h_ε * f, and concretely Hf(x) = lim_{ε→0} (1/π) ∫_{|t|>ε} f(x−t)/t dt in L^2-sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The integrand is the product of two L^2 functions on the set |t|>ε and is integrable by Schwarz. Use Theorem 8.24 (h_ε * f → Hf in L^2) to justify this concrete principal-value representation in the L^2 sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability of the '√' truncation function (Lemma 8.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific continuous odd function √(x) (constructed from 1/(π x) with truncation and smoothing near 0 and infinity) is integrable on R^1; in particular certain truncated kernels used in approximations belong to L^1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical lemma supplies an L^1 bound needed to control a piece in the decomposition of approximations to the Hilbert transform; check oddness and piecewise bounds to verify integrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation operator H_1 boundedness on L^2 and weak type (1,1) (Theorem 8.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define h_1 to be 1/(π x) for |x|≥1 and 0 for |x|<1, and H_1 f = h_1 * f (convolution) for f that is a sum of an L^1 and an L^2 function. Then ||H_1 f||_2 ≤ A ||f||_2 with A independent of f, and for every ξ>0, m({x: |H_1 f(x)|>ξ}) ≤ C ||f||_1 / ξ with C independent of ξ and f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives both strong L^2 boundedness and weak (1,1) control for the fixed truncation H_1. The proof uses decomposition of f into 'good' (g in L^∞∩L^2) and 'bad' (b supported on a union of intervals of small measure) parts via a Calderón–Zygmund-type decomposition, then controls H_1 g by L^2-boundedness and H_1 b by localized estimates using cancellation (zero total integral on each interval). Constants are obtained uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calderón–Zygmund (good/bad) decomposition properties for L^1 functions (construction used in Theorem 8.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f in L^1 and ξ>0, there exists a disjoint countable system of bounded open intervals {I_k} covering the set {x: f^*(x)>ξ} with properties: (i) (1/m(I_k)) ∫_{I_k} |f| ≤ 5 ξ, (ii) the sum of measures ∑ m(I_k) ≤ ||f||_1 / ξ, (iii) for each I_k with endpoints a<b we have ∫_{[a,b]} |f| ≤ 2 ξ m(I_k). Using these intervals define g and b=f−g with g bounded by 2ξ a.e. off the union and each b_k has mean zero on its interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decomposition is used to separate the L^1 function into a small L^∞-part and a localized part with cancellation. The construction relies on the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function and standard covering arguments; controlling H_1 on b uses the zero-average property and localized kernel estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hölder's inequality (Theorem 9.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,µ) is a measure space, 1≤p≤∞ and p0 is the dual index (1/p + 1/p0 =1), then for f∈L^p and g∈L^{p0}, the product fg is in L^1 and ||fg||_1 ≤ ||f||_p ||g||_{p0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the numerical Lemma 9.1 (Young-type convexity inequality) pointwise and integrate; handle endpoint cases (p=1 or p=∞) separately. This is the fundamental integral inequality used repeatedly (duality, interpolation, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minkowski's inequality (Theorem 9.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 1≤p≤∞ and f,g in L^p(X,µ), the sum f+g belongs to L^p and ||f+g||_p ≤ ||f||_p + ||g||_p (triangle inequality / Minkowski).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses Hölder's inequality for 1<p<∞ and trivial estimates for endpoints; this establishes that ||·||_p is a norm on equivalence classes, making L^p into a normed linear space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lp pseudonorm and construction of L^p spaces (definition and properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: For measurable f define ||f||_p = (∫ |f|^p dµ)^{1/p} for 1≤p<∞ (with the usual essential supremum for p=∞). These satisfy homogeneity, positivity, and the triangle inequality (Minkowski), so passing to equivalence classes gives the Banach space L^p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify homogeneity and positivity immediately; triangle inequality follows from Minkowski. One works with equivalence classes modulo a.e. equality. This construction underpins all later results about convergence, completeness, density, and duality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical convexity lemma used in Hölder (Lemma 9.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If s,t≥0 and α,β>0 with α+β=1 then s^α t^β ≤ α s + β t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by considering a convex function or by Lagrange multipliers; used pointwise (with appropriate powers) to derive Hölder's inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density of simple functions and inclusion relations (Proposition 9.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Indicator functions of finite-measure sets lie in every L^p; the smallest closed subspace containing such simple functions is L^p. (b) If 1≤p<∞ the simple functions (and L^p∩L^∞) are dense in L^p. (c) If 1≤p1≤p≤p2≤∞ then L^{p1} ∩ L^{p2} ⊆ L^p, with explicit containment depending on measure/essential supremum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use previous density results and truncation arguments: split f into parts where |f|≤1 and |f|>1 to show inclusion and density; finite-measure considerations appear in some embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolation inequality between L^{p1}, L^p, L^{p2} (Proposition 9.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 1≤p1<p<p2≤∞ and 1/p = t/p1 + (1−t)/p2 for some 0<t<1 then ||f||_p ≤ ||f||_{p1}^t ||f||_{p2}^{1−t}, with the p2=∞ case treated via the essential supremum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by applying Hölder with appropriately chosen exponents derived from interpolation parameter t. This provides an elementary Riesz–Thorin-like interpolation (for scalar norms) and is useful to bound intermediate norms from endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of L^p (Theorem 9.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 1≤p≤∞, L^p(X,µ) is complete: every Cauchy sequence in L^p has a subsequence converging pointwise a.e. to a function f in L^p, and the original sequence converges to f in L^p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof mirrors the p=1 case: extract a subsequence with summable L^p differences, show pointwise a.e. convergence of that subsequence, use dominated convergence/Cauchy control to show convergence in L^p. This theorem justifies Banach-space methods in L^p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak-type control via cancellation and kernel localization (technical estimate used in Theorem 8.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F∈L^1 vanishes off a bounded interval I, has total integral 0, and I* is the interval with same center and double length, then ∫_{x∉I*} |H_1 F(x)| dx ≤ C ||F||_1 for an absolute C (shown by estimating differences h_1(x−y)−h_1(x−y0)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This localized cancellation estimate is the crux of controlling the 'bad' part b in the Calderón–Zygmund decomposition when proving weak (1,1) bounds: exploit mean-zero of F on I and kernel smoothness/decay away from the interval to get uniform integrable tails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Hardy–Littlewood maximal function to localize L^1 mass (in Calderón–Zygmund decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the maximal function f^*(x)=sup_{h>0} (1/2h) ∫_{x−h}^{x+h} |f(t)| dt and set E={x : f^*(x) > ξ}; E is open and decomposes uniquely into disjoint open intervals I_k whose measures and averages satisfy the stated Calderón–Zygmund bounds. The measure m(E) is controlled by ||f||_1/ξ via the maximal theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard maximal-function based selection of 'bad' intervals. Use properties of f^* (maximal theorem and a.e. finiteness) to obtain the required size and measure estimates that underlie the decomposition into g+b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal-value integrals and limits in L^2 (interpretation of singular integrals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal-value singular integrals like the Hilbert transform are interpreted as limits of truncated convolutions h_ε * f in L^2; the limit exists in L^2 for f∈L^2 and the approximations are uniformly bounded in L^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extending singular integral operators beyond L^2, construct approximations with uniform L^2 bounds and then use weak-type (1,1) + interpolation or density to extend to other L^p. This is the strategy sketched here for H and its approximations h_ε.
